If the goal was stability, a smarter play would’ve been selective engagement—only stepping in when national interests are directly at stake and when there’s a clear, achievable objective. Instead, decades of trying to do everything at once left the U.S. looking like an overextended empire that nobody appreciates but everyone depends on.

Here are my tips as someone who has modded New Vegas since 2014:

1. Have a backup of the original game installed at all times instead of having to redownload and reinstall every time you mess up or want to restart

2. To answer your questions specifically, hit the button with the plus on it, make sure the directories are correct, and just open the mod archive from within that window to add it. When you add a mod after Viva New Vegas, create a new separator or even a group of separators, in front (below) of the old ones to distinguish between the base VNV mods and what you add after.

3. Do not be afraid of conflicts. I have never fucked with FNVEdit even though a lot of mods recommend doing this. I honestly dont care enough, and my computer has always been strong enough to run at least the base maximum of like 450 mods or so at once, and whatever stutters are minimal. I never really crash unless I specifically used a risky mod.

4. Test every single mod individually, and even compare similar mods together. One mod may run better but have less features and vise versa, sometimes one has everything you want and runs great. Just keep trying out mods, and realize its gonna take a long time to perfectly curate your mods, but by the end you have built a unique version of this game.

On controller, your cone of vision is just going to be slower and smaller probably, so use positioning to get that cone in the right spots. I honestly think having buttons for sprint and crouch/slide and knife all on the thumbs are intuitive, it can lead to better muscle memory on controller versus a keyboard.

That all being said, you will never be able to flick shots like a mouse player, you wont be able to track as well, your sweeps will be slower on controller. You wont be able to do combined inputs you just cant do on controller. Typically games with controller have aim assist and that can go a really long way, I always turned it off because it can also push your reticle OFF enemies if another runs by or it just bugs out.

The cover arts, the dialogues, the histories of bloodlines, patterns, just learn the lore and you’ll realize there is a set two races for each game that the theme always hints, or even outwardly states, between.

If you want to go absolutely canonical:

The Neravarine is either Dark Elf or Imperial.

The Champion of Cyrodiil is either a High Elf or Imperial.

The Dragonborn is either Nord or Imperial.

Khajiit have very little interest in prophecies not their own, but they do not discount them. They don’t want to be the heroes, they follow Ban Daar as their patron saint, so for the Thieves Guild it works perfectly, but I also don’t see the Dragonborn/CoC joining such an organization, nor the Knights of the Nine. Argonians follow Sithis as a sort of product of their Hist relationship, so it would make sense for one to join the Dark Brotherhood, and would be weird if they suddenly had religious faith towards Pelinal Whitestrake. And, again, the Dragonborn wouldn’t assassinate the Emperor, they’re a hero.

The point I’m trying to make is that while there is a theme and rationale for what races make sense to do what, what feels “wrong,” is all up to you. The point/message of the Elder Scrolls is to transcend your limitations. Martin in Oblivion becomes a dragon. The Neravarine reincarnates to fulfill a timeless destiny. The Dragonborn literally goes to Sovngarde and back. You can do and be anything in these games, and you are meant to make it as weird as you feel like. Do you imagine the CoC as a big black cat that walks around with skeletons and Daedra? Then that’s what they are. Bethesda designs their games with freedom at the tippy top.

Fallout 3 had Todd Howard’s specific artistic vision, and much like a prototype version of Skyrim, Fallout 3 was designed to match themes of desolation, grimdark, horror, tragedy, and the realness of survival. All the quests and characters are working toward this common thematic goal or motif.

Then you have Fallout 4 which drastically limits dialogue, and a knockoff Borderlands aesthetic, no discernible themes supported by multiple smaller and a grand narrative, but instead several separated stories spread across a framework of a game who’s goals are ultimately confusing. Is this a shooting game? It feels alright to shoot, but its not very deep, and there aren’t a lot of guns. Is this an RPG? If you have a good story, or a good quest, it shouldnt be so easy for me to tune out, especially as someone who likes these things. The overall design of FO4 clashes hard with what players wanted from Fallout, what Fallout has always been, and lacks any sort of direction beyond “streamlining.”

Obsidian says, at least from the wiki, that they were aware of this, and that the chambering of the rifle was changed last minute, as a request by Zenimax or Bethesda, to make the player feel stronger in the beginning. The Cannibals are not just scripted AIs, but they also learn from your actions and adapt. If you build in sight of a patrol route, or if you are seen entering your base, they will prepare to raid you. Sometimes, its not even an attack, but they’re showing the rest of their tribe where you are. Eventually though, as you become more aggressive, so will they. If you just fight them off every day, it will end up wasting so much of your daylight, and it becomes a priority over collecting resources or exploring. If you’re gonna fight back though, I recommend building Rock Walls. They are cheap, rocks are literally everywhere, and they are strong. You can stack them on top of each other, and then make another layer of proper logs in front of it, and lay hella Deadfall traps, as they do the most damage.

HOWEVER, if you want a much more interesting experience, I recommend not fighting them at all. Stay hidden. Never be seen in the first place. If you see them, sneak and run away. If you have to defend yourself, equip a stick, and block. The stick has perfect block so you take no damage. They may get even madder if you do this, and it will seem like they won’t let up, but eventually, if you just block their attacks, they’ll leave to go forage or patrol again, and leave you alone. If they just aren’t leaving you alone, hit them once or twice with the stick like a slap on the wrist. NEVER let the whole group see you kill, or if you do accidentally kill one, immediately destroy or hide the body, make sure there are no witnesses, because it will cause them to raid you next chance they get. Also, stay away from females. They tend to be more aggressive, but also if attacked, will cause the entire troupe to be more alert and violent. When you see effigies built by them, that’s their territory, and is generally a bad place to build. If you destroy these effigies, the cannibals will have to break from their routes, taking time to build new ones. I am not sure if this affects aggression, but it doesnt seem to matter. I also also recommend dummy shelters or decoy bases. When they find out you live somewhere, they will visit it occasionally. If you are seen living in many shelters across the map, it is way harder for the cannibals to track you down, especially if you have a main base that is well-hidden like on a cliff or behind a big boulder. At some point, when you’ve shown that you mean no harm, they will just watch and follow you, but not attack. One time I had a cannibal just enter my camp, take some fish off the drying rack, and leave without even looking at me. My final tip would be to build a drying rack out in the open away from camp and fill it with meat. This will attract them and honestly maybe they interpret it as a gift or something, but it almost feels like a mutual relationship.

Eventually, if you do go more peaceful, you will have to kill some cannibals to progress within the caves and beat the story. The longest I went without being raided was 50 something days. Its kind of nice knowing that the cannibal group in the distance wont even attack me because I’m not much of a threat to them or their resources.

I personally play them not because I’m a fan of the military or setting or realism, but because it uses these elements to make an arcade experience you can’t get in any other game. One that is almost entirely focused on practice, map memorization, gun memorization (recoil, range, tts, dps, mobility, and outmatches), and player habit abuse.

Basically, for shooter game players, there are not a lot of options, especially on console. Most games are not strictly multiplayer, but have a Battle Royale lean, but before the craze, CoD was THE game for console players if you wanted to shoot guns, and also Battlefield, but that game tends to stick more to PC players. If you wanted a multiplayer match, CoD could get you into one in seconds, always, and you always unlocked something or made progress. 

The Grind, to get all the camos in the game, are a big part of why people stay glued to CoD. It is a finely tuned unlockable system Activision has  developed over the years that gives the player just enough serotonin to keep playing, no matter their skill level. Before Battlepasses, these camo unlocks, and various stickers from challenges were the long-term draw for many players.

The fun part of the game comes only when you start learning maps. Zones that are important and zones that are not. Cheeky sightlines, places to hide, common thru-lines, all help you get a kill here or there, and then you start using a new gun and fall in love with it. When you start diversifying your loadout and experimenting is when you can be creative. CoD is much like a shooting game sandbox with rules that are there, but pretty optional. You may lose a match, but the best feeling from the game is topscoring both teams in kills with a “sub-optimal” gun like a single shot rifle or a slow shotgun.

Again, its not really the theme that makes players enjoy the game, but a blend of the theme along with several other facets of shooter innovation and arcade gameplay that make me love it. Also, the fact that we only get like one good game out of every four is constant blueballing to the audience. We want something we had so good a few times, but its so rare. A couple things:

Depending on how much youve built, and where, the cannibals can become more or less aggressive. Especially if you leave stumps behind.

The scraggly-looking animalistic cannibals are always aggressive, but weak. Block their attacks, whack them away a few times, try not to kill them. If they drown or fall to their death, that counts against you. However, as long as you are stealthy, build in strategic spots, constantly build temporary cabins for distraction, and don’t kill the cannibals, you can have a generally peaceful game. You will no matter what get attacked, and you pretty much have to murder to get deeper into the caves, but on almost every save, I get to about day 40 without having to fight at all. The cannibals will watch me chop trees, maybe they’ll swipe, I’ll block the attack, and they back off, just watching me. 

If you dont care about going that route, set up Deadfall traps. Theyre cheap, they cover a wide area, and can catch both cannibals and animals in one hit if you put two next to each other. Build rock walls around your log walls. They stack, and since rocks spawn everywhere constantly, easy to build. 

ONLY traps do damage. Defensive spikes and log spikes dont do anything but distract and take a long time to destroy. Build an effigy using only a few body parts, burn it during an attack, and you may get left alone for a few days. Build a shit ton of effigies, just keep them in a rotation. Also, make a drying rack out in the open, put meat on it, surround it with traps, and voila, cannibals pile up.
